newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major tries to defuse latest row on Europe.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major tries to defuse latest row on Europe.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major tried on Tuesday to draw a line under a row between his ministers over Europe that is threatening to tear the ruling Conservative party apart.

In a statement from his office and in comments to reporters, Major said the furore over remarks by finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Europe's plans to launch a single currency in 1999 was all a big misunderstanding.

"I am quite clear his views were misrepresented in the way in which they have been reported over the last couple of days," said Major, whose six years as prime minister have been bedevilled by divisions in his party over Europe.
He said that after speaking to Clarke, who is in Bermuda for a meeting of Commonwealth finance ministers, the government's position on a single currency remained entirely clear.

Clarke went further, calling reports of a cabinet rift a fabrication. He said he had been merely restating government policy when he told BBC radio on Sunday that it would be "pathetic" for Britain to wait and see how a European single currency developed before deciding whether to join.
"It seems to me the whole thing is a fuss about nothing... The whole thing has been a fabrication," Clarke told reporters.
Major was forced into damage limitation after junior Foreign Office minister Sir Nicholas Bonsor whipped up passions to fever pitch by accusing Clarke of departing from government policy.

With the Treasury forced to deny rumours in financial markets that Clarke had resigned, Major's office issued a statement saying both ministers fully supported the government's agreed policy on a single currency.
"The prime minister has made it clear that all ministers must adhere fully to the position agreed in cabinet," it said.
The government's official policy, which Major crafted to try to bridge the yawning divide between pro-Europeans and so-called Euro-sceptics in his party, is to keep all options open.

Euro-sceptics, who have been pressing Major to rule out joining the single currency during the five-year term of the next parliament, to be elected by May, were incensed that Clarke had expressed such overt support for a single currency.
Although some rank-and-file Conservatives called for Clarke to resign, political commentators were astonished that Bonsor should attack a much more senior colleague in public.

"I think he will be out of line with the view of the vast majority of the party and I think it is out of line with what the government policy has been as expressed before," Bonsor, who makes no secret of his Euro-sceptic views, told BBC radio.
Major said that Bonsor had given his interview based on misleading press reports of what Clarke, the cabinet's leading pro-European, had said.
"He now realises he was mistaken to speak on that misrepresentation," Major told reporters after talks with visiting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The latest squabbling -- extraordinary even by the standards of the Conservatives' long-running civil war on Europe -- bodes ill for Major's hopes of presenting a united front at the party's showpiece annual conference in two weeks' time.
The opposition Labour Party, 20 points ahead in opinion polls, said Bonsor had smashed the principle of collective government and brought the party's splits into the open.

"With such division and disunity now the dominant feature of this government, ministers are no longer fit or able to represent British interests in Europe or elsewhere," Gordon Brown, Labour's economics spokesman, said in a statement.
